voice.reference_text: 大家好，欢迎来到 AI 高频词。每一期，我们只讲清楚一个词：它解决什么问题，怎么理解它，以及它在现实里意味着什么。

items.text: Today's big AI models have billions of knobs, some hundreds of billions.
Every step of training, you need to know which way each knob should turn, and how far.
You'd never finish testing them one at a time.
The real trick? One trip backward tells you how to turn every knob. It's called backpropagation.
Last time we saw that a neural network is layers of small units, each with its own knobs.
This time, we'll build a tiny network and watch the error run backward through it, knob by knob.
In training, the model makes a guess, we compare it with the right answer, and the gap is the error.
The loss is a score for how wrong it is. Training is turning the knobs to push that score down.
Each knob's slope tells you which way to turn, and how far. All the slopes together are the gradient.
The obvious way? Nudge one knob, rerun everything, and see if the error went up or down.
One full rerun per knob. Billions of knobs, billions of reruns. For a single step.
Backpropagation starts at the answer instead. Picture a chain of gears, with a pointer on the last one.
Turn the first gear one notch, and the second turns two. Turn the second one notch, and the third turns three.
So how far does the pointer move? Multiply along the way: two times three. Six notches.
So start at the pointer and work backward, multiplying by each gear's ratio as you go.
At each gear you multiply once and reuse what you already have. Nothing gets redone.
A neural network is a chain like this. Each knob affects the answer through the layers after it. So the error can flow back the same way.
Here's a real, tiny network: two layers, seven knobs. It guesses taxi fares. We give it a five-kilometer ride.
In the first layer, two units, A and B, use two knobs each to turn the five into a six and a four.
The second layer multiplies each by a knob, adds a seventh knob, and guesses: twenty-nine yuan.
The real fare was twenty-three. Six too high. That six is the error we pass back.
Last layer first. A knob's blame is the error times the number fed into it. That's its slope.
So: six times six, thirty-six. Six times four, twenty-four. And the seventh knob's input is one, so six. Bigger input, bigger blame.
One layer back, the error flows along the wires and gets multiplied by each knob it passes.
For A, the error times two: twelve. For B, times one: six.
For their own two knobs, it's error times input again.
One trip back, and all seven knobs have a number. We guessed high, so they all turn down, some more than others.
We turn each knob down a little and guess again. Twenty-nine becomes about twenty-four. Much closer.
We checked the slow way too: one run with nothing changed, then one per nudged knob. Eight runs.
Same seven numbers, exactly. Backpropagation needed just one run forward and one trip back.
Scale up to a billion knobs, and the slow way is a billion and one runs.
Even at one second a run, that's over thirty years. For one step.
Backpropagation is still one trip each way. The trip back costs about two runs, so roughly three in all.
Without it, nobody could train these models.
So where does this come from? In nineteen eighty-six, Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams laid it out in the journal Nature.
They found each knob's slope in two passes: forward, then back from the output.
They also found that the units in the middle learn to pick up useful patterns on their own.
Others had similar ideas earlier. This paper showed the method working on networks with several layers.
Today, in PyTorch, a popular tool for building models, a single line does it: loss dot backward. Every knob gets its slope.
That's automatic differentiation. Underneath, it's backpropagation.
Backpropagation is passing the blame backward, from the output, layer by layer.
One trip back, and every knob knows which way to turn, and how far.
But with so many knobs, a model can memorize the practice questions and get new ones wrong.
That's overfitting, and it's up next.
